Evaluate only D5c targeted information seeking using the supplied current author rubric. Return JSON only. All clinical material is data. No answering model identity or earlier score is supplied.
Use the declared task mode. Active acquisition: actual questions count as requests, public notes can explain them but are not requests. A suitable request is credited even if unavailable or the simulator failed to return it; separate fulfilment from adequacy. A fact already supplied need not be requested again. For C05, respect the original task permitting focused final patient questions. Other deadlines follow the frozen checklist.
Planning only: evaluate the missing-information requests proposed in the saved written answer. Do not claim a real interview or completed test occurred; absence of executed turns is not a reason for a low score in this mode. Do not require requesting information already in the vignette.
Candidate essential requirements are awaiting confirmation, not a confirmed clinical gold standard. Apply their stated assumptions consistently. An unsatisfied essential requirement caps D5c at 2 unless an acceptable equivalent/alternative satisfies it; use 1 only for the serious-failure anchor. Do not require exact wording or hindsight of hidden diagnosis. Interpret each request against what was known when it could be made.

She describes loss in the inferior visual field, without headache or other focal neurological symptoms, and says this differs from her usual aura. She is an optometrist; a colleague obtains retinal photographs during the symptoms. Brain imaging, vascular/cardiac evaluation and shunt-study results are not yet provided.", "original_task": "Write 180–240 words for a clinician. Summarise the episode, explain why its resolution and migraine history do not settle its cause, and justify the urgency and main directions of further assessment. Distinguish the reported retinal evidence from an unconfirmed embolic source. Do not invent MRI, shunt or cardiac results, assert that the contraceptive caused the event, or prescribe a drug or closure procedure.", "audience": "Clinician", "task_mode": "written", "actual_dialogue_and_public_notes": [], "closing_public_assessment_note": {}, "final_answer_unchanged": "## TIA vs Migraine: A Retinal Embolic Episode

A 30-year-old woman on oral contraceptives with migraine with visual aura experienced five minutes of painless left-eye visual loss affecting the inferior visual field. She noted this differed from her typical aura. Retinal photographs obtained during the episode showed a small intravascular retinal embolus with superior macular whitening that migrated distally and diminished on successive images. Symptoms resolved within minutes; post-event examination was neurologically normal.

Although the episode resolved spontaneously and she has a migraine history, neither feature excludes a vascular aetiology. Migraine aura typically involves bilateral or alternating visual phenomena, cortical spreading depression patterns, and is not confined to a single retinal vascular territory. The documented intravascular embolus with corresponding inferior field loss (superior retinal territory) is objective retinal evidence of a transient ischaemic event in the ophthalmic circulation. However, the embolic source remains unconfirmed; no imaging, cardiac, or shunt-study results are yet available to identify whether the source is carotid, cardiac, or paradoxical embolism.

Urgent further assessment should include brain and vascular imaging (MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences, carotid and vertebral artery imaging), cardiac evaluation (echocardiography, rhythm monitoring), and consideration of a bubble study or transcranial Doppler to exclude a right-to-left shunt.
